items.title: FG committed ​‌‌‍‍‍⁠‍⁠⁠‌⁠⁠‌‌‍⁠​‍‌​to research, innovation commercialisation — Minister

original_payload.original_title: FG committed ​‌‌‍‍‍⁠‍⁠⁠‌⁠⁠‌‌‍⁠​‍‌​to research, innovation commercialisation — Minister
original_payload.original_body:
Science & Tech  FG committed ​‌‌‍‍‍⁠‍⁠⁠‌⁠⁠‌‌‍⁠​‍‌​to research, innovation commercialisation — Minister
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   1 hour ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Ijeoma Olorunfemi
The Federal Government says it is intensifying efforts to commercialise research and innovation outcomes and connect them with industry to drive economic development.
The Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Udeh, said this on Wednesday in Abuja.
He spoke at the 3rd Quarter 2026 Stakeholders and Citizens Ministerial Engagement on the Implementation of Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) Policy Projects and Programmes.
Udeh said the initiative, tagged “Energise Commercialisation Now,” was designed to bridge the gap among research institutions, innovators and the market.
He said the government recognised that Nigeria had no shortage of ideas, research outputs and innovations, but many remained on the shelves of academic and research institutions without being developed into commercial products.
According to him, the initiative is focused on supporting researchers and innovators to move from concepts and prototypes to marketable products, industries and revenue-generating ventures.
Udeh said the initiative was inaugurated in Kano for the North-West in April, where research and innovation outcomes with investment potential were identified across the seven states.
He said the ministry was preparing to extend the initiative to other geopolitical zones, with the North-Central and South-South expected to be among the next areas of engagement.
The minister also said that the process for establishing the National Research and Innovation Development Fund (NRIDF) had progressed, following Federal Executive Council approval and the transmission of a bill to the National Assembly.
He said the proposed fund would provide sustainable financing for research and innovation beyond government remittances.
Udeh said the fund would help address the financing gap that often prevented innovations from progressing from prototype to commercialisation.
He also announced the commencement of the ministry’s Youth and Student Innovation Programme.
According to him, it is aimed at equipping young Nigerians and students with digital and technology skills for entrepreneurship, employment and innovation.
Dr Olushola Odusanya, Director-General, National Centre for Technology Management (NACETEM), said the centre was focusing on research that could translate into products, services and solutions to societal challenges.
He said NACETEM was also developing middle-level technical manpower needed for industrialisation, particularly in welding, foundry, industrial electrical work and mechatronics.
He advocated stronger measurement of Nigeria’s investment in science and technology, technical manpower and innovation outputs to align the country with global standards.
The engagement brought together stakeholders from government agencies, research institutions, academia, industry and other parts of the STI ecosystem.( NAN ) www.nannews.ng
Edited by Uche Anunne

items.title: Mozambique: CTA calls for mineral resource industrialisation and local production of components for megaprojects

original_payload.original_title: Mozambique: CTA calls for mineral resource industrialisation and local production of components for megaprojects
original_payload.original_body:
Photo: CTA The Vice-President of the Confederation of Economic Associations of Mozambique (CTA), Onório Manuel, has called for stronger national industrialisation through the creation of industrial parks, the attraction of investment and the local production of components for megaprojects operating in Mozambique.
During a panel entitled “Investment Incentives and the Industrialisation of Mineral Resources in Mozambique”, held as part of CAVAME-d 2026, Onório Manuel highlighted ongoing progress in Nampula province, particularly the Topuito Industrial Park, a project initiated around five years ago in association with Kenmare, which aims to attract investors and stimulate industrial activity.
The CTA Vice-President also noted that efforts are under way to develop new industrial parks in coordination with the World Bank, with the aim of creating conditions for the establishment of production facilities and expanding local processing capacity.
“In the 21st century, it makes no sense for us to continue importing industrial parts that we can produce locally,” was the central message of his remarks, as he highlighted the need for megaprojects to strengthen their links with national industry by promoting the local production of parts and components used in their operations.
This approach aims to reduce dependence on imports, stimulate productive investment, develop domestic suppliers and ensure that the exploitation of mineral resources translates into greater added value for the Mozambican economy.
Onório Manuel’s remarks reinforce the CTA’s position in support of industrialisation based on infrastructure, investment, local content and the development of national productive capacity as pillars of business competitiveness, job creation and sustainable economic development.
Source:  CTA / Press Release

items.title: The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu

original_payload.original_title: The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu
original_payload.original_body:
On September 26, five leading members of Israel’s self-styled Zionist opposition signed a non-aggression pact, seeking to oust incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 election.
Gathered at the Tel Aviv home of opposition leader Yair Lapid were his co-runner, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of Beyachad; former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the new Yashar party; Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party; and Avigdor Liberman, head of the Yisrael Beiteinu party.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items    list 1 of 4  How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
list 2 of 4  Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears
list 3 of 4  Israeli opposition signal foreign policy change in style, but not substance
list 4 of 4  If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians?
end of list
In the statement of principles published after the hours-long meeting, the leaders said, “Despite ideological differences among us, the formation of a Zionist, statesmanlike government dedicated to repair and reconstruction is our shared overarching goal.”
However, whether they offer meaningful change in substance as well as style, or which one of them might lead a future coalition, remains  open to question .
From left, Israeli opposition leaders Yair Lapid, Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman meet on September 26, 2026 [Courtesy of Yair Lapid via X]   With the exception of Golan, all take a fundamentally right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges.
None is committed to establishing a Palestinian state, with only the Democrats acknowledging it as a distant, unspecified goal. None, Golan included, accepts that Israel’s war on Gaza amounts to genocide or that it has committed war crimes in killing more than  74,000 people  there. Nor has any questioned Israeli military actions against Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Qatar and Iran, instead reserving criticism mostly for how those actions have allowed Israel to be perceived internationally.

Paris, France –  More than 70,000 police officers and gendarmes are set to be deployed across France as the country braces for a new round of protests against deteriorating school conditions and the rising cost of living.
French authorities have made clear they are determined to prevent Saturday’s  demonstrations  from descending into the violence that erupted last weekend.

items.title: Telenovela Índico passa ocupar espaço na grelha da Stv

original_payload.original_title: Telenovela Índico passa ocupar espaço na grelha da Stv
original_payload.original_body:
A telenovela indico antes exibida na Stv Play, prepara-se para ganhar uma nova montra. O produto cinematográfico 100% nacional passa a ser exibido no ecrã da STV a partir de 1 de Novembro. A novidade foi anunciada esta quinta-feira.
Não havia tapete vermelho, nem uma cerimónia aberta ao público. O momento foi sobretudo de comunicação interna.
A direcção da “Índico”, uma telenovela genuinamente moçambicana, reuniu actores e equipa técnica para partilhar oficialmente uma novidade, a passagem da telenovela para o sinal aberto da Stv.
A telenovela que até aqui está disponível na STV Play, passa a ocupar também um espaço no sinal aberto a partir deste domingo.
Para Joanett Rombe, que concebeu o projecto, a “oportunidade que a Stv oferece, é uma vitória,” que valorizam os cinco anos de produção e gravação.
Mais do que a mudança de plataforma, a chegada à STV é encarada como ponto mais alto para o alcance dos objectivos da equipa da produção: quebra de paradigmas históricos.
“Concebemos este projecto para quebrar a ideia de que novela para ser atraente deve ser de fora. Nós temos capacidade para fazer isto e mais,” expressou a atriz com mais de 30 anos de carreira.
“Não faz sentido nos 30 anos de representação nos limitarmos a conteúdos de fora.”
E para quem esteve envolvido na produção, o momento representa também uma espécie de recompensa pelo trabalho realizado longe dos grandes holofotes.
Beatriz Rombe, fez parte da equipe de produção, conta que o maior desafio foi mobilizar financiamento para a concretização do projecto. Havia pouco empresariado acreditando.
“Diziam que só vão apoiar quando a novela começar a passar na Stv, ninguém esperava isso. Hoje estamos gratos, fomos honrados.”
Para os actores, a notícia de exibição do produto audiovisual na Stv foi recebida com entusiasmo.
Tânica Mabica e Cília Chirinda expressaram ao O País a sua emoção, com expectativa de, o projecto, atrair atenção de mais pessoas.
A decisão da Stv, segundo Isabel Manhiça, diretora do canal, está alinhada com a sua aposta em conteúdos nacionais e apoio às artes e cultura.
“Queremos trazer conteúdo diferente e que seja nosso, para o verão e a quadra festiva. Esperamos que este produto, que é nacional, seja marcante para os moçambicanos”
A telenovela passa a ser exibida ao domingo, a partir de 1 de Novembro, antecedendo o jornal da noite.

items.title: Bantè : deux Togolais arrêtés avec plus de 1 000 boules de chanvre indien

original_payload.original_title: Bantè : deux Togolais arrêtés avec plus de 1 000 boules de chanvre indien
original_payload.original_body:
Deux ressortissants togolais ont été arrêtés dans la nuit du dimanche 11 octobre 2026 à Bantè, alors qu’ils transportaient une importante quantité de chanvre indien à bord d’un minibus. La fouille du véhicule a permis aux policiers de découvrir 1 031 boules de cette substance, dissimulées dans des sacs.
Salomon AGADA (Stag)
L’opération a été menée aux environs de 1 heure du matin par le commissariat d’arrondissement de Bantè, à la suite d’un renseignement transmis par son homologue de Bassila. L’alerte faisait état d’un véhicule suspect, initialement signalé pour le transport présumé de munitions de calibre 12. Informé de la situation, le responsable du commissariat de Bantè a mobilisé une équipe pour effectuer des contrôles sur l’axe routier concerné. Le dispositif mis en place a permis d’intercepter le minibus Mazda après une course-poursuite. Les deux occupants, des hommes quadragénaires originaires de Kouloumbé, au Togo, ont alors été arrêtés. La fouille du véhicule a conduit à la découverte de 1 031 boules de chanvre indien réparties dans onze sacs de jute. Pour dissimuler la cargaison et en atténuer les odeurs, les occupants avaient utilisé des sacs contenant de la sciure, des copeaux et des écorces d’arbres. Lors de son interrogatoire, l’un des suspects a déclaré que le chargement avait été effectué à Aworo, dans la commune de Bassila. La marchandise devait ensuite être acheminée vers Kétou, dans le département du Plateau. Les deux hommes ont été placés en détention. Ils devront répondre des faits qui leur sont reprochés devant le procureur de la République

items.title: Les pays en développement assommés par le poids des intérêts de la dette publique

original_payload.original_title: Les pays en développement assommés par le poids des intérêts de la dette publique
original_payload.original_body:
Les pays en développement assommés par le poids des intérêts de la dette publique
En 2025, le remboursement des intérêts liés à la dette publique a approché 1 000 milliards de dollars. Un chiffre qui donne le tournis, alors que l'agence de l'ONU pour le commerce et le développement (Cnuced) s'inquiète, dans un rapport, du poids de la dette, en particulier pour les pays en développement.
Publié le :  10/10/2026 - 22:58
1 min     Temps de lecture
Le coût de la dette dans les pays en développement explose et grève les budgets publics au détriment de priorités de développement telles que la santé et l'éducation, selon la Cnuced.        REUTERS/Yuriko Nakao
Par :
RFI
Publicité
«  L'argent que les pays en développement consacrent à payer les intérêts de leur dette publique n'est pas disponible pour financer la santé, l'éducation et les autres services publics essentiels  », souligne la Cnuced, dans un rapport paru jeudi 8 octobre.
La dette cumulée des pays les plus pauvres dépasse désormais les 7 500 milliards de dollars, soit près de 70% de la dette publique mondiale. Or, prêter à ces pays est considéré comme plus risqué par les marchés, qui leur imposent donc des taux d'intérêts plus élevés. En moyenne les pays développés empruntent à un taux de 3,6% ; les pays en développement, eux, à un taux de plus de 6%.
À lire aussi  Les laissés-pour-compte de la croissance économique
Plus inquiétant encore : depuis 2022, le poids cumulé des intérêts à rembourser dépasse la somme des nouveaux prêts obtenus par les pays en développement, parce que l'aide au développement s'effrite et que les bailleurs privés se montrent de plus en plus allergiques aux risques.  Autrement dit, les pays en développement empruntent désormais pour rembourser les prêts précédents, et non plus pour investir. En   Afrique  , par exemple, la part des finances publiques que les gouvernements consacrent au seul remboursement de la dette a doublé en 15 ans .

items.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph

original_payload.original_title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
original_payload.original_body:
Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders.
Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon.
Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women.
Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours.
“It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.”
After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology.
When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent.
But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees.
Aya turned to her older brother Yasser.
Seventeen years her senior, Yasser was a lawyer with his own practice, a wife and three children: Adnan, nine, Ahmad, seven, and three-year-old Ilaf. He helped support their parents and hoped one day to teach law at university.
“I used to always tell him, ‘You're a second father to me,’ because he was so kind to me, just like my father,” Aya says.
Aya remembers a summer's day in August 2023. Yasser, still dressed in his smart work clothes, came to take her from Nuseirat to the Islamic University of Gaza.
"Together, we went from department to department, trying to find a course that was affordable and that I would enjoy," she says.
Professors suggested engineering. But when they came out, Aya told Yasser she couldn't imagine herself studying computers or becoming an engineer.
“I could picture myself wearing a white coat, that's all,” she told him.
They tried health sciences next.
“Maybe I could study something in the medical field,” Aya suggested. “I really liked medical laboratory sciences.”
Yasser knew that his sister was giving up the version of university she had imagined. But he refused to let her see the decision as the end of something.
"Perhaps it's for the best," he told her. "Maybe one day you'll become a doctor in the field you choose to specialise in. You don't have to be a medical doctor; you could become a university professor with a PhD."
Then, he offered her a thought that has stayed with her. "He told me, 'Sometimes what is withheld from us can be better for us than what is given to us,' and I believe him."
Afterwards, he took her to Al-Taboun restaurant for lunch, while they kept talking about university and the choices available.
Aya enrolled in medical laboratory sciences, and Yasser bought her books and supplies. University had barely completed its first week when the war began.
A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house.
The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted.
She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to.
Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there.
On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food.
On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32.
Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation.
When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one.
“I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says.
Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained.
After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things.
"My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me."
She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat.
original_payload.original_summary: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them.
original_payload.author: Lina Ghassan Abu Zayed

items.title: Maradi : 1 266 candidats prennent part à l’examen unique de certification en santé

original_payload.original_title: Maradi : 1 266 candidats prennent part à l’examen unique de certification en santé
original_payload.original_body:
Maradi, 3 Oct (ANP) – Le Gouverneur de la région de Maradi, le Contrôleur Général de Police Issoufou Mamane, a procédé ce samedi 3 octobre 2026 au CEG 3 de Maradi au lancement du concours de certification unique en santé.
Au total, 1 266 candidats prennent part à ce concours de certification unique en santé dans la région de Maradi.
Prenant la parole à cette occasion le Gouverneur de la région de Maradi a affirmé que toutes les dispositions ont été prises pour assurer le bon déroulement de l’examen. Il a rappelé que cette certification vise à permettre aux Nigériens, quelle que soit l’école de santé fréquentée, d’obtenir un diplôme reconnu par l’État.
Le Gouverneur a invité les candidats à compter sur leurs propres connaissances, à éviter toute tricherie et à ne pas prendre de risques pour un examen qui peut être repris en cas d’échec. Il leur a souhaité bonne chance et bon courage.
Pour sa part Le Directeur régional de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique de Maradi, Dr Idi Moussa, a précisé que 1.266 candidats issus de 11 écoles de santé prennent part à l’examen unique de certification en santé, lancé ce samedi 3 octobre 2026.
Les candidats sont répartis entre plusieurs filières, dont 808 agents de santé de base, 296 licenciés en soins infirmiers, 139 licenciés en soins obstétricaux, 19 techniciens de laboratoire et 4 licenciés en santé environnementale. Au total, 34 salles sont mobilisées pour les épreuves, qui se déroulent dans de bonnes conditions.
Selon Dr Idi Moussa, cet examen vise à renforcer le contrôle et la qualité de la formation des professionnels de santé. Il est organisé chaque année sur l’ensemble du territoire national sous le contrôle du ministère de la Santé.
Rappelons que cet examen s’inscrit dans le cadre des décrets pris par le Gouvernement pour renforcer le contrôle et la qualité de la formation dans le secteur de la santé.

items.title: NPRGS: Turning FG’s skills training into sustainable livelihoods

original_payload.original_title: NPRGS: Turning FG’s skills training into sustainable livelihoods
original_payload.original_body:
Features  NPRGS: Turning FG’s skills training into sustainable livelihoods
By  Muhyideen Jimoh   ·   24 seconds ago   ·  9 min read
✓
✓
By Muhyideen Jimoh
For a young Nigerian struggling to find a job, a sewing machine could provide an entry point into entrepreneurship, generate income and help support a family.
For another, a laptop could open opportunities in Artificial Intelligence (AI), graphic design and other areas of the digital economy.
These possibilities underpin the Federal Government’s National Poverty Reduction with Growth Strategy (NPRGS), which seeks to equip Nigerians with practical skills, productive tools and opportunities to earn sustainable livelihoods.
However, poverty reduction requires more than short-term interventions.
The critical question is whether such programmes can help beneficiaries establish viable businesses, secure employment and sustain their incomes.
The initiative comes against the backdrop of Nigeria’s wider skills-development challenge, as government and other stakeholders seek to bridge gaps between education, vocational training and labour-market demands.
For instance, the Federal Ministry of Education’s Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) initiative reported more than 1.3 million applications, 160,000 youths matched to training and over 73,000 enrolled, alongside more than 1,700 accredited training centres.
Although these figures relate to a separate initiative, they indicate substantial demand for vocational training and underscore the need to connect training opportunities with employment and entrepreneurship.
More broadly, technical and vocational education can provide pathways into employment and self-employment.
Its effectiveness, however, depends partly on relevant courses, qualified instructors, access to equipment and links with employers and markets.
Similarly, aspiring entrepreneurs may require start-up capital, mentorship and access to customers to turn newly acquired skills into sustainable sources of income.
Against this background, the NPRGS seeks to combine vocational training with certification, productive equipment and entrepreneurship support.
At the centre of the intervention is Dr Abiola Arogundade, Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Technical, Vocational and Entrepreneurship Education (TVEE).
Arogundade’s work focuses on translating the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda into practical opportunities for Nigerians through skills acquisition, entrepreneurship and technology-driven empowerment.
In support of the initiative, the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Sen. Abubakar Atiku Bagudu, commended the programme and reaffirmed the ministry’s commitment to interventions that align with Nigeria’s national development priorities and improve citizens’ livelihoods.
“The NPRGS is a cornerstone of our national development agenda. By focusing on skills, we’re tackling poverty at the root and unlocking Nigeria’s human capital,” he said.
The programme forms part of the administration’s broader poverty-reduction ambition.
According to the State House, the NPRGS is intended to contribute to the Federal Government’s target of lifting 100 million Nigerians out of poverty within 10 years.
Within this wider strategy, the skills intervention has a stated target of reaching five million young Nigerians.
A September 2026 report by a leading media outlet put the timeframe for that target at four years.
This distinction is important because the number of people trained or provided with equipment does not automatically translate into the number lifted out of poverty.
Explaining the objective, Arogundade said: “The objective is to lift more than five million Nigerians out of poverty.
“What we are doing, and what the President wants us to achieve is to move as many people out of poverty through skills acquisition, empowerment, entrepreneurship and technology-driven opportunities.”
To advance these objectives, the programme combines vocational trades with digital skills, offering participants different routes into employment and self-employment.
Its training areas include digital technology, fashion design, makeup artistry, solar installation and agriculture-related enterprises, reflecting the range of skills through which beneficiaries could pursue income-generating activities.
In Abuja, more than 300 beneficiaries received training in cybersecurity, web development and solar installation, alongside laptops and certificates.
Beyond the FCT, the programme has extended to Oyo State, with Enugu and Kebbi among the next locations planned for implementation.
The Oyo State phase further demonstrated the programme’s combination of technical instruction and practical empowerment to help beneficiaries apply their newly acquired skills.
At the programme’s graduation ceremony in Ibadan on Oct. 9, 700 beneficiaries were empowered through its training and digital empowerment components.
At the event, Arogundade urged beneficiaries to extend the benefits of the intervention to others, emphasising the potential for knowledge-sharing to multiply its impact.
“Don’t use it as a one-man solution or one-man empowerment. There’s a multiplier effect. Train your neighbours, train your community people, and also continue to impact and learn more,” she said.
Beyond the programme’s overall figures, participants’ experiences offer an insight into how the training could influence their career paths and livelihood prospects.
Miss Balikis Soliu, a makeup artistry participant and University of Ilorin mathematics graduate, said the opportunity had opened a new path towards entrepreneurship and an improved livelihood.
Although she already had some basic knowledge of makeup before the training, Soliu said the theoretical and practical sessions had greatly expanded her skills and understanding.
“It has been a very interesting journey and a genuine transfer of knowledge,” she said.
According to Soliu, the trainers ensured that participants acquired practical skills to help them establish successful careers in the beauty industry.
“I teach mathematics. So now, combining teaching and makeup artistry will help me because I have been living only on salaries.
“I can’t wait to own my own space and become a very good makeup artist,” she said.
Similarly, another participant, Mr Akintunde Fabiyi, a teacher of Mathematics and Science, said the technology training had broadened his understanding of digital tools, graphic design and AI.
He said he had been exposed to new concepts and technological tools, especially design software for creating professional designs and developing brands.
In addition, Fabiyi highlighted the importance of AI, noting that he now understood how to apply emerging AI tools in graphic design efficiently and productively.
He commended President Bola Tinubu for his effectiveness, adding that participants had already covered significant areas of technology and design within seven days.
Nevertheless, Fabiyi acknowledged that the 10-day training period could not accommodate every aspect of the programme’s syllabus.
He said this had reinforced the need for participants to remain committed to continuous learning and skill development after the training.
Fabiyi said he planned to “level up and scale up” by practising the skills acquired consistently, learning new techniques and taking advantage of available opportunities.
He said his goal was to improve his professional prospects and income while contributing to society and serving as a good ambassador of Nigeria.
For Mr Ogunyemi Aduragbemi, a fashion design trainee, the programme offered an opportunity to return to a trade he had previously practised.
Aduragbemi said he had left fashion design for trading because he could not afford the necessary equipment.
Consequently, he expressed excitement about receiving equipment at the end of the training, saying this would enable him to combine trading with fashion design and improve his income.
Meanwhile, the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, commended Arogundade and the Federal Government for the initiative, calling it a game changer in efforts to reduce poverty.
“It’s a very good initiative, and we are very proud of Arogundade and this initiative.
“I would also like to encourage many people in her position to emulate her, because this will go a long way in empowering people and reducing poverty in our society,” the Olubadan said.
The programme is also expected to extend to Enugu and Kebbi states, broadening access to vocational and technology-based training.
In Enugu, Gov. Peter Mbah has pledged support for the programme ahead of its planned entry into the Coal City on Oct. 28.
The governor acknowledged the programme’s potential to expand economic opportunities and generate wider development benefits.
In addition to vocational training for young people, the intervention promotes digital inclusion through technology-based learning opportunities for students.
More than 100 HP laptops have been provided to schools, alongside training opportunities in robotics and AI.
Beneficiary institutions include Government Secondary School, Tudun-Wada, Wuse Zone 4, and Government Science and Technical College, Garki, Abuja.
Through these activities, the initiative seeks to expose students to technologies that could support future employment, entrepreneurship and innovation.
Nevertheless, access to equipment and introductory training alone may not guarantee sustained participation in the digital economy.
Continued learning, mentorship and opportunities to apply acquired skills will also be important.
Similarly, vocational training may not automatically translate into stable earnings without access to start-up capital, customers, suitable working conditions and markets for beneficiaries’ products and services.
These considerations are important in assessing the programme’s poverty-reduction ambitions, especially as implementation expands to more states and reaches different groups of Nigerians.
For the Tinubu administration, the target of lifting more than five million young Nigerians out of poverty is substantial.
Achieving it will require sustained implementation, effective partnerships and measurable results.
Consequently, the programme’s long-term success will depend on whether training translates into productive work, viable businesses and lasting improvements in household livelihoods.
Arogundade’s approach brings together skills development, equipment provision, business grants and evaluation, potentially strengthening the link between empowerment initiatives and measurable economic outcomes.
From sewing machines and makeup kits to laptops and solar technology, the strategy seeks to provide practical resources through which beneficiaries can pursue productive livelihoods.
While Arogundade has urged beneficiaries to extend their skills to others, the wider test of the NPRGS will be whether the training translates into sustainable livelihoods.
As the programme expands to more states, its impact will depend on beneficiaries’ ability to apply their skills, establish viable businesses and secure reliable sources of income.
Tracking these outcomes will be essential to determine how far the intervention is contributing to the Federal Government’s poverty-reduction objectives.
Ultimately, the programme’s value will lie not only in the number of Nigerians trained, but also in the economic opportunities they create for themselves, their families and their communities. (NANFeatures)

items.title: Conflits agropastoraux au Bénin : Urgence d’accélérer la recherche de solution définitive au phénomène

original_payload.original_title: Conflits agropastoraux au Bénin : Urgence d’accélérer la recherche de solution définitive au phénomène
original_payload.original_body:
Éleveur peulh (photo générée pour LNT)
Conflits agropastoraux au Bénin : Urgence d’accélérer la recherche de solution définitive au phénomène
20/10/2026    par    Tognissè Dahandé
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le sang a encore coulé dans le nord du Bénin. Mardi 20 octobre 2026, à Kika, dans la commune de Tchaourou, un agriculteur s’est vu trancher la main à la machette par un éleveur pour avoir simplement tenté de chasser un troupeau de bœufs en train de dévaster son champ. Ce drame effroyable, qui prive un père de famille de son outil de travail et de son avenir, survient alors que les chiffres officiels affichent une nette baisse des tensions. Mais sur le terrain, l’urgence demeure absolue : il faut transformer les avancées administratives en une paix réelle et durable.
À Kika, l’émotion et la colère sont vives. Comment un simple différend lié à la dévastation d’une parcelle de maïs peut-il basculer dans une telle barbarie ? Cet acte d’une violence inouïe rappelle avec fracas que la transhumance reste une bombe à retardement dans nos campagnes.
Pourtant, au niveau national, la situation s’améliore. Selon les données de la récente revue de performance du secteur agricole présentées à Cotonou, les conflits entre agriculteurs sédentaires et éleveurs transhumants ont enregistré un recul de 42,8 % en 2025. Un progrès indéniable, fruit des efforts de l’État et de ses partenaires.
Pour comprendre la persistance de ces drames, il faut observer les facteurs de friction récurrents. Au premier rang figurent la divagation des troupeaux et le piétinement des cultures (maïs, mil, niébé, riz), cause majeure qui représente plus de la moitié des litiges enregistrés. À cela s’ajoutent les effets du changement climatique (assèchement précoce des mares, raréfaction des pâturages), qui intensifient la compétition pour la terre et l’eau, ainsi que les divergences sur la délimitation des espaces agricoles et pastoraux.
Les élus locaux : acteurs de première ligne dans la résolution des crises
Face à cet engrenage, les élus locaux (maires, chefs de village et d’arrondissement) s’imposent comme les véritables gardiens de la paix sociale. Étant au plus près des réalités du terrain, ce sont eux qui réceptionnent les premières plaintes, apaisent les esprits et empêchent que les querelles ne dégénèrent en affrontements communautaires.
L’exemple de la commune de Lalo, dans le Couffo, est à ce titre un modèle du genre. Anticipant les risques de la saison, la maire Pélagie Gowui a réuni en octobre 2026 l’ensemble des acteurs clés (représentants des éleveurs, agriculteurs, forces de sécurité et élus locaux), autour d’une table pour instaurer une veille pastorale pacifique. Par le rappel des règles (couloirs de passage, sanctions), mais surtout par l’instauration d’un dialogue direct et permanent, la municipalité démontre que l’action locale est la clé de voûte de la prévention.
Cette centralité des exécutifs communaux est également reconnue par le pouvoir central. Lors de la tournée gouvernementale à Covè en juin 2024, conduite par le Garde des Sceaux Yvon Déchénou, aux côtés des ministres de l’Intérieur et de la Décentralisation, le gouvernement est venu échanger directement avec les élus locaux du Zou. Rappelant que l’État ne tolérera plus les violences systématiques, la délégation a promis un accompagnement renforcé des mairies et affirmer que la vulgarisation des textes réglementaires et du Code pastoral en langues locales devait impérativement s’appuyer sur les autorités communales pour être efficace.
Digitalisation et fermeté : doter les communes d’outils modernes
Pour épauler efficacement les élus locaux dans leur mission de médiation, la réponse doit aussi devenir technologique et judiciaire. Le ministère de l’Agriculture, de l’Élevage et de la Pêche (MAEP) a annoncé la mise en place d’un recensement général du bétail couplé à l’identification des troupeaux par des étiquettes auriculaires à code QR. Grâce à la plateforme  Agratime , les autorités locales et les forces de l’ordre pourront identifier en un clic les propriétaires d’animaux fautifs, mettant fin à l’anonymat qui nourrit l’impunité.
Parallèlement, la justice doit poursuivre sa descente vers les communes. Comme promis par le gouvernement à Covè, l’implication accrue des Procureurs de la République et des Officiers de Police Judiciaire aux côtés des maires permettra de lever les blocages administratifs qui freinent parfois le règlement impartial des litiges.
Le drame de Kika doit marquer un tournant définitif. Si la baisse de 42,8 % des conflits prouve que la démarche globale porte ses fruits, le basculement vers le « zéro conflit » passe inévitablement par un soutien accru aux élus locaux. Ce sont eux, grâce à leur proximité et leur légitimité, qui sauront faire du Code pastoral une réalité vivante et transformer la transhumance en un vecteur de cohabitation harmonieuse.

items.title: Jonathan commends ex-deputy governors’ forum for promoting national unity

original_payload.original_title: Jonathan commends ex-deputy governors’ forum for promoting national unity
original_payload.original_body:
General News  Jonathan commends ex-deputy governors’ forum for promoting national unity
By  Tosin Kolade   ·   45 minutes ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Emmanuel Oloniruha
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has commended the Forum of Former Deputy Governors of Nigeria (FFDGN) for promoting national unity, democratic governance and economic cooperation.
Jonathan gave the commendation on Monday during a visit to the forum’s office in Abuja, where he expressed satisfaction with its facilities and efforts to preserve the history of former deputy governors.
“I am quite impressed with what I have seen. Today is my first day here, and I did not know that we had such a gigantic structure with well-furnished offices,” he said.
Recalling his tenure as deputy governor in 1999, Jonathan said the facility reflected the forum’s history and contributions over the years.
He said former deputy governors could continue to contribute to national development beyond politics.
“What you are doing goes beyond politics. It is also about commerce and industry, and linking Nigeria with the rest of the world,” he said.
Jonathan urged members to sustain the forum’s activities and contributions to national development.
Earlier, the Chairman of FFDGN, Dr Chris Akomas, said the idea of establishing the forum originated from Jonathan, who proposed that former deputy governors unite to speak with one voice.
Akomas said the forum had continued to grow, with members committed to promoting national progress, stability, unity and democratic governance.
He said the forum’s annual conference would reflect its commitment to the welfare of Nigerians, irrespective of their state of origin, religion or political affiliation.
Akomas said collective responsibility and cooperation were essential to building the country Nigerians aspired to have.
“Everybody talks about the Nigerian dream, but it is our responsibility to make it a reality. We must do our best to ensure that this dream becomes a positive reality that benefits everyone,” he said.
He appreciated Jonathan and others who had supported the forum, saying their contributions had helped sustain its activities.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the forum is a non-partisan body comprising former deputy governors from the country’s 36 states.
It serves as a platform for members to share governance experiences, promote national development and offer policy recommendations on issues affecting Nigeria’s democratic governance and socio-economic development. (NAN)

items.title: Burkina Faso : un budget 2027 fixé à 4 200 milliards FCFA et d'importants chantiers validés

original_payload.original_title: Burkina Faso : un budget 2027 fixé à 4 200 milliards FCFA et d'importants chantiers validés
original_payload.original_body:
Afrique
Burkina Faso : un budget 2027 fixé à 4 200 milliards FCFA et d'importants chantiers validés
Réuni sous la présidence du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le Conseil des ministres a examiné l'avant-projet de budget 2027, acté la création de la Ligue de la souveraineté et validé de nouveaux projets sanitaires.
Alwihda Info
08 oct. 2026
Burkina Faso : un budget 2027 fixé à 4 200 milliards FCFA et d'importants chantiers validés. © PR BF
Réuni le jeudi 8 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou sous la présidence du chef de l'État, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le Conseil des ministres a arrêté les grandes lignes de l'avant-projet de loi de finances pour l'exercice 2027, tout en validant d'importants projets dans les domaines du sport et de la santé.
Présenté par le ministre de l'Économie et des Finances, Aboubakar Nacanabo, le budget 2027 s'équilibre à 4 200 milliards de FCFA de recettes pour 4 800 milliards de FCFA de dépenses. Cet instrument financier, adossé au plan R.E.L.A.N.C.E., vise à stimuler la croissance économique en soutenant l'agriculture, l'industrialisation, l'équipement des forces armées et les services sociaux de base. Le texte, qui sera soumis à l'Assemblée législative du Peuple, intègre également des mesures d'allègement fiscal concernant la filière avicole, les agences de voyages et les sociétés d'État.
Sur le plan sportif, le gouvernement a entériné la création de « La Ligue de la souveraineté », une nouvelle compétition de football portée par le ministère des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l'Emploi. Selon la ministre Annick Lydie Djouma Pikbougoum/Zingué Ouattara, ce championnat ambitionne de décentraliser l'élite sportive à travers le territoire. Vingt équipes y participeront, réparties entre les différentes régions du pays, avec une représentation spécifique pour le Kadiogo et le Guiriko.
Enfin, dans le secteur sanitaire, le Conseil a validé la réalisation de plusieurs infrastructures majeures pilotées par le Bureau National des Grands Projets. L'Initiative présidentielle pour la santé se traduira par la construction et l'équipement de 20 centres médicaux communaux, de 20 maternités modernes, de quatre blocs opératoires pour l'hôpital militaire Halassane-Coulibaly ainsi que par la création d'un institut du cœur.

items.title: Malaria cases surge amid acute drug shortages in West Darfur

original_payload.original_title: Malaria cases surge amid acute drug shortages in West Darfur
original_payload.original_body:
The medical director of El Geneina Hospital in Sudan’s West Darfur State, Dr. Al-Shafie Salih Younis, has warned of acute shortages of malaria medication, including intravenous treatments and tablets, amid a growing influx of patients and increased demand for healthcare services.
He called on international organizations operating in the health sector to urgently intervene and provide the necessary medicines.
“Demand for malaria medication is high as increasing numbers of patients seek treatment at the hospital.” He said. “The shortage is exacerbating the suffering of patients and putting them at risk of deteriorating health. Mortality rates could rise if the drug shortages persist and adequate medical supplies are not secured.”
Separately, Dr. Bakhit Hassan, director-general of the medical complex, warned of the serious complications malaria can cause, explaining that the disease can affect the brain, kidneys, liver and joints.
“Residents should undergo medical testing and receive a proper diagnosis before taking medication because malaria symptoms can resemble those of other illnesses.” He said.
Dr. Hassan also criticized what he described as disruptions in the pharmaceutical supply chain, saying some hospitals were obtaining medicines from unknown sources. He further warned that improper storage practices could cause medicines to deteriorate and lose their efficacy.
He also pointed to the presence of inadequately trained healthcare personnel, stressing the need for stronger oversight of drug quality and improvements in healthcare services.
The warnings come amid growing concerns over the deterioration of health conditions in West Darfur, where medicine shortages and mounting pressure on healthcare facilities underscore the urgent need for intervention to ensure access to treatment and the safety and reliability of pharmaceutical supplies.

items.title: Ce que Zelensky redoute si Washington passait officiellement du côté de Poutine

original_payload.original_title: Ce que Zelensky redoute si Washington passait officiellement du côté de Poutine
original_payload.original_body:
Volodymyr Zelensky - Photo : Présidence Ukrainienne
Ce que Zelensky redoute si Washington passait officiellement du côté de Poutine
18/10/2026    par    Charly Hessoun
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Quatre ans et huit mois après le début de la guerre, le président ukrainien  Volodymyr Zelensky  lance un avertissement à Washington. Dimanche 18 octobre 2026, il a déclaré que  l’Ukraine  ne pourrait pas tenir si les  États-Unis  prenaient officiellement le parti de la Russie. Il y voit  « une tragédie, une erreur historique et une grande tragédie » . Ces propos suivent plusieurs décisions de  Donald Trump  qui ont allégé la pression sur Moscou et que Kiev critique ouvertement.
Zelensky  s’exprimait dans l’émission  Meet the Press  de la chaîne américaine   NBC  .  « Si les États-Unis prennent officiellement le parti de la Russie, bien sûr, nous ne l’emporterons pas. Nous ne pourrons pas tenir » , a-t-il affirmé.
Il ne dit pas pour autant que ce basculement a eu lieu.  « Nous voulons lui faire confiance » , a-t-il dit à propos de   Trump  , avant d’ajouter :  « J’espère qu’il changera ses décisions, car je pense que ce sont toutes des erreurs » . Interrogé sur le statut d’allié du président américain, il a répondu :  « Je l’espère » .
Diesel russe, Starlink, renseignement : les décisions que Kiev conteste
Trump a d’abord assoupli des sanctions visant la  Russie . La semaine dernière, il a annoncé un accord avec  Vladimir Poutine  pour vendre sur le marché mondial des centaines de milliers de tonnes de diesel russe, afin de calmer la hausse des carburants aux  États-Unis.
Zelensky  rejette cet argument. Selon lui, l’accord n’aura pas  « d’influence réelle »  sur les prix américains, car ceux-ci montent à cause du blocage du détroit d’Ormuz. Il affirme surtout que cet accord  « renforcera Poutine dans sa volonté de nous occuper » .
Le président ukrainien dénonce aussi le bridage de  Starlink , qui sert à guider une partie de ses drones.  « C’était un message du gouvernement américain » , a-t-il assuré. Si  Trump  levait la restriction,  « cela fonctionnera immédiatement comme avant » , a-t-il ajouté.
Le partage de renseignement américain a lui aussi été bloqué pendant trois jours lors d’attaques de missiles balistiques, avant d’être rétabli, d’après  Zelensky . Des responsables européens et ukrainiens ont indiqué à NBC y voir une pression pour arracher des concessions à Kiev, alors que les négociations de paix sont au point mort. Zelensky affirme avoir été  « très honnête »  avec Trump, qui l’avait jugé plus difficile à gérer que Poutine.
Sur X, le dirigeant ukrainien a publié le même jour un bilan chiffré :  « Depuis que le président américain a annoncé le cessez-le-feu énergétique il y a une semaine, la Russie a délibérément attaqué 76 fois les secteurs ukrainiens de l’énergie, du pétrole et du gaz » .

items.title: Kokoyé Assogba Cécile, chanteuse, compositrice et slameuse : Une voix qui appelle à une prise de conscience

original_payload.original_title: Kokoyé Assogba Cécile, chanteuse, compositrice et slameuse : Une voix qui appelle à une prise de conscience
original_payload.original_body:
Culture
Kokoyé Assogba Cécile, chanteuse, compositrice et slameuse : Une voix qui appelle à une prise de conscience
ONEP NE
9 octobre 2026
L’artiste Kokoyé Assogba Cécile
Partager vers les réseaux
La scène urbaine nigérienne s’affiche comme le reflet d’une génération en quête d’identité et de justice sociale. Longtemps cachées dans l’ombre des traditions, les femmes bousculent ce code afin de faire résonner leur voix.
Née le 22 novembre 2002 à Niamey, Kokoyé Assogba Cécile est une artiste chanteuse, compositrice et slameuse, résidente à Maradi. Poussée par sa passion pour la musique dès l’enfance, elle a, du jour au lendemain, transformé cet élan en un engagement.
Avec un style Rnb engagé et conscient, elle cumule trois casquettes pour être une artiste complète et indépendante. Elle rédige ses textes et choisit le sens du rythme des mots. Ensuite, elle crée l’univers sonores, structure les mélodies et apporte sa voix afin de sublimer le texte et la musique.
Pour Cécile, la musique urbaine constitue un canal d’expression qui lui permet de véhiculer des messages, d’aborder des sujets sensibles afin de dénoncer des injustices sociales, tout en restant proche de la réalité et du quotidien de ceux qui l’écoutent.
Inspirée des artistes comme le duo du groupe MDM, Alradik ou Safiah, la chanteuse Cécile explore, dans ses productions, des thèmes liés à la paix, la cohésion sociale, l’autonomisation de la femme et l’éducation.
Le quotidien exerce une grande influence sur ses écrits, car, dit-elle, ces thèmes sont nés de plusieurs constats faits dans son entourage. Ainsi, elle transforme en slam ou en chant ses observations.
Dans son clip “femme battante”, Cécile défend avec vivacité la cause féminine et dans “Sahélien”, elle fait l’éloge des origines du Niger, tout en invitant la population à une prise de conscience pour mieux construire ce pays.
La chanteuse Cécile a été plusieurs fois finaliste lors de grands concours sans pour autant toucher la crête. Au lieu de céder à l’échec, elle a doublé d’efforts jusqu’à occuper la 4e place lors de la finale de Sarkin Waka édition 2026, une expérience qui l’a particulièrement marquée, tant sur le plan artistique que personnel.  « Je reviendrai l’année prochaine avec plus de force pour soulever le trophée », a-t-elle promis, déterminante.
Cependant, cette slameuse fait face à des difficultés qui freinent l’évolution de sa carrière artistique. « L’une des principales difficultés que je rencontre est le fait de ne pas être installée dans la capitale. Cela fait que je rate beaucoup d’opportunités qui vont me permettre de participer à de grands événements pour développer ma carrière au-delà des frontières », se plaint-t-elle, tout en évoquant également la difficulté liée au manque de visibilité. Ce qui dissimule sa voix.
De même, le fait d’être une femme dans le milieu musical représente un défi pour Cécile, car, selon elle, la femme chanteuse est mal jugée par la société.
Par ailleurs, la jeune artiste constate une approbation appréciable des autorités locales et certaines organisations internationales pour la musique urbaine. Mais, elle indique qu’au niveau de la population, l’évolution de la musique urbaine est freinée par une faible consommation de cet art. «Nous avons beaucoup de talents au Niger. Il est donc important que le public consomme davantage la musique locale afin de savoir quels messages les artistes véhiculent à travers cet art pour un changement collectif», a-t-elle souligné.
Afin de se hisser dans l’univers de la musique urbaine, Cécile s’active à réaliser ses projets dont l’enrégistrement d’un album, l’organisation d’un Café Slam à Maradi et une tournée.
L’artiste Cécile exprime sa gratitude à ses fans pour leur soutien et leurs encouragements, tout en adressant un message aux jeunes qui désirent emprunter le chemin musical d’être ambitieux et persévérants.
Zouladeini A. Razinatou  (ONEP)

items.title: Tribal clashes contained after six killed in South Darfur

original_payload.original_title: Tribal clashes contained after six killed in South Darfur
original_payload.original_body:
Authorities in Sudan’s South Darfur State said they had contained tribal clashes that killed six people and wounded others following a dispute over a motorcycle between two clans of the Beni Halba tribe.
The clashes occurred over the weekend in the Gunu area of Ed al-Fursan Locality. The dispute escalated into an armed confrontation, leaving six people dead and others injured on both sides.
Salah al-Moj, head of the civil administration in South Darfur State, told Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday that the state security committee had travelled to Ed al-Fursan to assess the incident and its security implications.
“The state security committee visited Ed al-Fursan following the incidents and met with the relevant people and bodies to discuss measures to resolve the issue,” he said.
He said the committee also met with the locality’s security committee to establish how the violence unfolded and review measures to address the crisis.
Al-Moj said the committee had reviewed security arrangements and efforts to resolve the dispute through customary tribal mechanisms, including the payment of blood compensation to the families of those killed.
The committee also directed the rival groups to disperse their armed gatherings and ordered an increased deployment of regular security forces to restore state authority in the locality, he said.
South Darfur police director Lieutenant Colonel Khalid Mohamed Nur said the situation had been brought under control.
He said police had responded to residents’ demands for additional personnel and equipment, including vehicles, weapons and uniforms.
“We send our sincere condolences to the families of those killed in the tribal conflict, and we would like to tell the public that the situation has been contained,” Nur said.
He acknowledged that police in the area face challenges and lack some equipment and transport, adding that plans are under way to provide vehicles, weapons, uniforms and other necessities to strengthen their ability to maintain security.
“We urge the people of Ed al-Fursan to ensure that such incidents do not occur again, and we thank the community leaders for their wisdom and patience,” he said.
South Darfur is among the states controlled by the Sudan Foundation Alliance (Tasis), a parallel administration aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan’s army since April 2023.
Tasis announced the formation of a parallel administration in areas under its control in July 2025. RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti, heads its presidential council, while civilian politician Mohamed Hassan al-Taishi serves as prime minister.

original_payload.original_title: Guinea's ex-Constitutional Court president sentenced to seven years in jail
original_payload.original_body:
Guinea
The former president of Guinea's Constitutional Court, Mohamed Lamine Bangoura, was sentenced on Wednesday to seven years in prison by an anti-graft court.
It convicted him of illicit enrichment, corruption, embezzlement of over $20 million dollars in public funds, and money laundering.
Bangoura was also sentenced to a heavy fine and substantial damages to be paid to the state jointly with his two co-defendants, who are both fugitives.

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire: un cadre du PPA-CI, Sébastien Dano Djédjé, inculpé et placé sous contrôle judiciaire

original_payload.original_title: Côte d'Ivoire: un cadre du PPA-CI, Sébastien Dano Djédjé, inculpé et placé sous contrôle judiciaire
original_payload.original_body:
Côte d'Ivoire: un cadre du PPA-CI, Sébastien Dano Djédjé, inculpé et placé sous contrôle judiciaire
Président du Conseil stratégique et politique du Parti des peuples africains-Côte d'Ivoire, Sébastien Dano Djédjé a été inculpé de 17 chefs d'accusation - dont ceux d'« actes terroristes », d'« assassinat » ou d'« atteinte à la sureté de l’État » - à l'issue de sa convocation à la section antiterroriste d'Abidjan, lundi 12 octobre. Depuis un an, plusieurs hauts responsables de la formation de Laurent Gbagbo sont visés par des procédures judiciaires.
Publié le :  13/10/2026 - 06:57
2 min     Temps de lecture
Sébastien Dano Djédjé lors d'une conférence de presse, le 30 décembre 2025.        © Abdoul Aziz Diallo / RFI
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondante à Abidjan,   Fanny Noaro-Kabré
Un mois après le placement sous mandat de dépôt de Justin Koné Katinan en   Côte d'Ivoire  , un autre cadre du Parti des peuples africains-Côte d'Ivoire (PPA-CI), le parti de Laurent Gbagbo, a été inculpé et placé sous contrôle judiciaire, lundi 12 octobre.
À lire aussi  Côte d'Ivoire: l’opposant et ex-ministre Justin Koné Katinan placé sous mandat de dépôt
Convoqué dans la matinée à la section antiterroriste à Abidjan, Sébastien Dano Djédjé a été inculpé, à l'issue de deux heures d'audition, de 17 chefs d’accusation parmi lesquels ceux d'« actes terroristes », d'« assassinat » ou d'« atteinte à la sureté de l’État ». Selon son avocate, Me Roseline Aka Sérikpa, certains sont en lien avec les troubles électoraux survenus lors de la présidentielle de 2025, sans qu'elle ne précise lesquels. Le président du Conseil stratégique et politique du PPA-CI a toutefois pu regagner son domicile.
Sébastien Dano Djédjé rejoint ainsi la liste des cadres du PPA-CI visés par des procédures judiciaires depuis un an. Tel est par exemple le cas du 4e vice-président du parti, Justin Koné Katinan, donc, mais aussi de Damana Pickass, un proche de   Laurent Gbagbo   notamment accusé « d'actes terroristes », qui est incarcéré depuis le mois de novembre dernier.
Si cette situation conduit certains militants du PPA-CI à dénoncer des arrestations politiques, les autorités rejettent, elles, cette accusation : «  Ce sont des prisonniers de droit commun qui ont commis des délits prévus par la loi  » commentait ainsi ce week-end une source gouvernementale auprès de RFI.
À lire aussi  Côte d’Ivoire: arrestation d'un bras droit de Laurent Gbagbo

items.title: Cristiano Ronaldo a gagné plus de 2 milliards de dollars en carrière, un record pour un athlète en activité

original_payload.original_title: Cristiano Ronaldo a gagné plus de 2 milliards de dollars en carrière, un record pour un athlète en activité
original_payload.original_body:
Cristiano Ronaldo (Photo Facebook)
Cristiano Ronaldo a gagné plus de 2 milliards de dollars en carrière, un record pour un athlète en activité
22/10/2026    par    Francis Noude
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Cristiano Ronaldo  est le premier athlète en activité à dépasser les 2 milliards de dollars de revenus de carrière, un cap franchi en 2026 selon le classement des footballeurs les mieux payés publié par   Forbes  . L’attaquant portugais d’ Al-Nassr , club basé en Arabie saoudite, a touché environ 300 millions de dollars sur les douze derniers mois:  « Cristiano Ronaldo, superstar du football, mène la liste pour la quatrième année consécutive, avec environ 300 millions de dollars, soit sa meilleure année jamais mesurée par Forbes »  affirme le magazine. Notons que ce montant le place une nouvelle fois devant son éternel rival  Lionel Messi , avec qui il occupe les deux premières places du classement pour la 12e fois en 13 ans.
Revenus de carrière et fortune nette : deux notions distinctes
Il faut préciser que les 2 milliards de dollars correspondent à des gains cumulés avant impôts et frais d’agents, et non à un patrimoine. En effet,  Forbes  évalue la fortune nette de   Ronaldo   à 1,2 milliard de dollars. Rappelons qu’il avait déjà été présenté comme le premier footballeur milliardaire en octobre 2025, après la prolongation de son contrat avec Al-Nassr jusqu’en 2027, estimée à plus de 400 millions de dollars sur deux ans.
Mais, sur la dernière saison, 235 millions de dollars proviennent de son salaire et de ses primes, et environ 65 millions de ses contrats commerciaux, notamment avec  Nike ,  Binance  et  Perplexity . Pour Forbes,  « Cristiano Ronaldo est sans doute l’athlète le plus populaire au monde, avec près d’un milliard d’abonnés cumulés sur Instagram, Facebook et X… Al-Nassr verse à Ronaldo plus de 200 millions de dollars par an » .
Messi reste derrière, mais pas loin
Notons que le Portugais précède de peu l’Argentin, qui joue à Inter Miami. Forbes a indiqué que  « Messi a gagné environ 1,8 milliard de dollars sur et en dehors des terrains durant sa carrière, avant impôts et frais d’agents » . Ainsi l’écart avec  Ronaldo  avoisine donc 200 millions de dollars, et il pourrait se maintenir. Pour la saison 2026-2027, le magazine prévoit en effet environ 250 millions de dollars de salaire pour Ronaldo, auxquels s’ajouteraient 50 millions de revenus extra-sportifs.

items.title: PAAU School Fees Crisis: Prof. Ogbo, Focus On Your Responsibilities As Vice-Chancellor Or Fully Join Politics! By A. O. Augustine

original_payload.original_title: PAAU School Fees Crisis: Prof. Ogbo, Focus On Your Responsibilities As Vice-Chancellor Or Fully Join Politics! By A. O. Augustine
original_payload.original_body:
Ordinarily, I would not have considered it necessary to devote my time and energy to commenting on the conduct of the Vice-Chancellor of Prince Abubakar Audu University, Anyigba, Prof. Ogbo. However, after listening to your defence of the Kogi State Government's decision to harmonise tuition fees across the state's three universities, I can no longer remain silent.
With all due respect, your defence was not only unconvincing but also a disappointing attempt to justify a policy whose implications for students, parents, and the future of public education deserve far more serious consideration.
Professor Ogbo, you cannot defend a controversial government policy simply because you occupy an office that depends on the government. Your primary responsibility is to the university, its students, its staff, and the pursuit of knowledge not to the political interests of those who appointed you.
I am particularly disappointed because you are not an outsider to the institution. You passed through the same university as a student, served as a lecturer, and eventually rose to the position of Vice-Chancellor. You should, therefore, understand the realities of the institution, its peculiar challenges, and the struggles of the students who depend on it for their academic and professional advancement.
Unfortunately, your recent posture raises serious questions about whether you are protecting the interests of the university or merely defending the political establishment.
YOUR APPOINTMENT MUST NOT BECOME A DEBT TO YOUR POLITICAL SPONSORS
When news of your return to the university surfaced after your tenure as Rector of Kogi State Polytechnic, I was not particularly surprised.
Having personally participated in campaigning for the government of the day, I viewed your appointment through the lens of political reward and patronage. That perception may be disputed, but it is precisely the kind of public concern that political appointments can generate when the circumstances surrounding them are not adequately explained.
However, an appointment to lead a university should be about competence, institutional development, academic excellence, and the capacity to improve the lives of students and staff.
The office of Vice-Chancellor is not a political settlement, and the university is not a campaign headquarters.
Once appointed, a Vice-Chancellor must rise above partisan considerations and demonstrate independence of thought, administrative fairness, and commitment to the institution's long-term interests.
If your appointment was based on merit, let your performance speak for itself. If you believe you are qualified to lead the institution, demonstrate that qualification through policies that improve academic standards, protect students' welfare, promote research, and create an environment where learning can thrive.
You owe the university that responsibility.
FROM EVICTING LEGITIMATE BUSINESSES TO MAKING THE UNIVERSITY ENVIRONMENT MORE DIFFICULT
I was not disappointed when, shortly after assuming office, you reportedly began taking steps that forced people who had been conducting legitimate businesses within the university environment to leave.
The question is simple: what informed those decisions, and what alternatives were provided to the people affected?
Universities must maintain order, enforce regulations, and ensure that commercial activities do not interfere with academic work. Nobody disputes that responsibility. However, administrative authority must be exercised with fairness, transparency, and consideration for the livelihoods of those affected.
If the decision was necessary, the university ought to explain its rationale and demonstrate that the affected parties were treated fairly.
What is particularly troubling is the tendency to justify controversial decisions by pointing to what other universities have done. The fact that another institution adopted a similar policy does not automatically make that policy appropriate for Prince Abubakar Audu University.
Different universities operate under different circumstances, with different infrastructure, student populations, and local economic realities.
Professor Ogbo, leadership is not about copying other institutions blindly. It is about making decisions that serve the best interests of the institution you have been entrusted to lead.
HUMAN RIGHTS ARE NOT OPTIONAL, EVEN WITHIN A UNIVERSITY
Another issue that deserves serious attention is the reported public parading of suspected individuals, including the display of their faces in connection with allegations of cultism.
Let us be clear: cultism, violence, intimidation, and criminal activities have no place in any university. The management of every institution has a responsibility to protect students and staff from threats to their safety.
However, the fight against criminality must not become an excuse to disregard fundamental human rights.
Under Section 36(5) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999, as amended, every person charged with a criminal offence is presumed innocent until proved guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.
A university administration is not a court of law. Its management cannot substitute public accusations for due process, nor should suspected individuals be presented to the public in a manner that suggests their guilt has already been established.
If individuals are suspected of cult-related activities, the appropriate course is to document the allegations, cooperate with law-enforcement agencies, and allow the relevant authorities to investigate and prosecute where the evidence supports it.
Professor Ogbo, the university must not become a place where accusation is treated as conviction and administrative power substitutes for the rule of law.
The objective should be to protect the university community while preserving the dignity and rights of every individual.
WHY IS FEE HARMONISATION MORE URGENT THAN STAFF WELFARE?
This brings us to the central issue: the harmonisation of tuition fees across the three state-owned universities.
Professor Ogbo, one question you must answer is this: why does the harmonisation of students' fees appear to command such urgency when questions about the harmonisation of staff salaries, allowances, and conditions of service across the state's institutions remain legitimate matters for public discussion?
If harmonisation is being presented as a policy of fairness and uniformity, then the government and the university management must explain the principles guiding its application.
Why should uniformity be emphasised when determining what students pay, without equally demonstrating a commitment to fairness in other aspects of the public university system?
Students are not merely revenue sources. They are young Nigerians whose parents and guardians make enormous sacrifices to keep them in school. Many families are already struggling with the rising costs of food, transportation, accommodation, and other basic necessities.
Any policy that increases their financial burden deserves careful examination.
A government may have legitimate reasons for reviewing university fees, including the need to fund infrastructure, improve teaching facilities, and sustain academic programmes. However, those reasons must be supported by transparent explanations, meaningful consultation, and appropriate measures to protect students from being priced out of education.
The responsibility of a university administrator is not to defend every government decision, but to ensure that government policies affecting the university are examined through the lens of education, fairness, and institutional sustainability.
If the harmonisation policy is genuinely beneficial, present the evidence. Explain how it was designed, how its implications were assessed, and what safeguards exist for students from low-income households.
Do not expect the university community to accept a policy merely because the government has announced it.
TWENTY YEARS AGAINST TWO YEARS: WHAT EXACTLY ARE WE HARMONISING?
There is also a fundamental question about the fairness of harmonising fees across institutions with significantly different histories, operational realities, and financial structures.
How can a university that has operated for more than two decades be placed on the same fee structure as an institution that has existed for only about two years without a clear explanation of the factors considered?
The age of an institution alone does not determine what its students should pay. Nevertheless, differences in institutional maturity, infrastructure, programme offerings, operating costs, and funding arrangements must be examined before a uniform policy is imposed.
A proper harmonisation exercise should be based on evidence, not political convenience.
It should explain the disparities among the institutions, the rationale for the proposed fee structure, the expected impact on students, and the measures being taken to ensure that no institution or category of student is unfairly disadvantaged.
As Hon. Gudaje reportedly asked, "Which kind of harmonisation is that?"
It is a question that deserves a substantive answer, not a defensive reaction.
Harmonisation should mean fairness, consistency, and a transparent framework. It must not become a convenient label for transferring the financial burden of public education to struggling parents.
PROFESSOR OGBO, THE UNIVERSITY IS BIGGER THAN YOUR POLITICAL AMBITIONS
There is a growing perception among some observers that your administration is more concerned with political calculations than with the difficult business of managing a university.
I am not in a position to determine your private political ambitions, and I will not pretend that allegations about your intentions are established facts. However, public officeholders must understand that their conduct can generate public perceptions that they may not necessarily welcome.
If you have political ambitions beyond your current office, there is nothing inherently wrong with aspiring to serve in another capacity, subject to the law and applicable rules.
But you must not allow such ambitions, real or perceived, to overshadow your responsibilities as Vice-Chancellor.
The university is not a stepping stone that should be sacrificed for political advancement. It is an institution that shapes the future of generations.
If you are interested in partisan politics, be clear about your priorities and respect the boundaries of your present office. If you intend to remain Vice-Chancellor, then give the university your full attention.
You cannot have the university community wondering whether your decisions are driven by educational considerations or political calculations.
THERE WERE VICE-CHANCELLORS BEFORE YOU, AND THERE WILL BE OTHERS AFTER YOU
One of the greatest mistakes any public officeholder can make is to believe that an institution begins and ends with them.
Prince Abubakar Audu University existed before your appointment. It has been led by other Vice-Chancellors, each with their own strengths, weaknesses, and contributions. It will continue to exist after your tenure ends.
You are a temporary custodian of a permanent institution.
Your duty is to leave the university stronger than you met it—not to create an environment in which students, staff, business operators, and other members of the university community feel that their interests are secondary to the demands of your administration.
History will not remember you merely because you occupied the office of Vice-Chancellor. It will judge your tenure by the policies you implemented, the academic environment you created, the welfare of students and staff, the quality of graduates produced, and the institutional legacy you left behind.
No appointment lasts forever. No political patron remains in power forever.
And no administrator should mistake temporary authority for personal ownership of an institution.
MY FINAL WORD TO PROFESSOR OGBO
Professor Ogbo, this is not a personal invitation to hostility. It is a call for accountability from someone who believes that Prince Abubakar Audu University deserves better than a leadership style that appears, to its critics, excessively defensive of government policies and insufficiently responsive to the concerns of the university community.
You have an opportunity to correct that perception.
Re-examine policies that impose avoidable burdens on students. Explain the rationale behind fee harmonisation. Protect the rights of suspected individuals. Ensure that disciplinary procedures are fair and transparent. Address legitimate concerns about staff welfare. And demonstrate, through your actions, that the university's interests come before political considerations.
You must also understand that criticism is not necessarily hostility, and disagreement is not necessarily an attempt to undermine your authority.
Those who question your policies are not automatically your enemies. Some may be asking the questions that responsible leadership ought to answer.
Professor Ogbo, stop treating the defence of government decisions as the ultimate test of loyalty. Your first responsibility is to the university you lead.
If you believe your future lies in partisan politics, pursue that ambition through the appropriate channels and subject to the applicable rules. But while you occupy the office of Vice-Chancellor, give the institution the leadership it deserves.
Do not play politics with the future of our students.
Do not sacrifice institutional progress on the altar of political loyalty.
And do not mistake the silence of some members of the university community for universal approval.
We are watching. We are asking questions. And we will continue to demand accountability.
Prince Abubakar Audu University is bigger than any individual, bigger than any political party, and bigger than any administration.
It belongs to the people whose taxes sustain it, the students whose dreams depend on it, and the generations whose future it is expected to shape.
Professor Ogbo, the choice is yours: rise to the responsibility of being Vice-Chancellor, or stop allowing political calculations to overshadow the office you currently occupy.
The university deserves leadership, not political theatre. And history will be the ultimate judge.
